VM Support Plan: A Programmable Query Layer

StatusDiscussion complete, not yet proposed/planned (on 2026-10-28 the user proposed “adding VM support to db for more flexibility” and the evaluation was completed; this page is the authoritative record of the conclusion). The positioning in one sentence: do not introduce SQL; introduce programmable query logic — the bytecode is SA's own SAB, and modules keep using qmod's hash addressing. Prerequisites: SAB interpreter stability cleanup + a VM fuel metering specification (the same VM investment shared with the sangx logic-layer plugin).

Precedent and current state

  • SQLite is essentially a bytecode VM: SQL is first compiled to VDBE bytecode and then executed; its flexibility comes from that virtual machine, except that the bytecode is not open to users. This plan amounts to opening up that layer, with bytecode that is native to the SA ecosystem: SAB.
  • qmod is already a prototype: the plugin already has a mechanism for “precompiled query modules executed by hash” (sa db exec <hash>); VM-ifying it generalizes qmod from a few fixed query shapes to arbitrary query modules written in SLA, with the addressing and dispatch mechanism unchanged.
  • The hard boundary in the current state is the read-handle API: adding a new query shape = adding a native API + releasing a new version of the plugin. The primary benefit of VM-ification is removing that boundary.

Flexibility benefits

  • New query shapes without a release: predicates, aggregations, and join logic can be written as bytecode modules, with the host and plugin binaries unchanged.
  • Computation pushdown: filtering/aggregation execute next to the read snapshot, avoiding row-by-row data movement across the FFI; modules are addressed by hash, so they can be hot-swapped, versioned, and A/B tested.
  • Stored-procedure-like capabilities: stored procedures/triggers/materialized views — which MySQL has and SQLite is weak at — can be supplied by VM modules, and modules are constrained by capability (they can only touch tables they are authorized for), which is cleaner than MySQL stored procedures' full-privilege model.
  • Ecosystem compounding: sangx's logic-layer plugin, the planned sardis scripting surface, and db's query modules share the same VM and the same capability model — the VM's stability and performance investment is spread across three products.

Design discipline (keep these, or it stops being this plugin)

  • The schema is always fixed at compile time: the VM may only touch query logic. If this line is not held, the plugin will slowly grow into a second general-purpose database and lose its founding trade-off of “compile-time schema, no runtime parsing”.
  • Two-tier execution: the VM only orchestrates; column-operation primitives (vectorized operations such as sum/filter/count) remain as native externs for modules to call. Hot modules keep an AOT escape hatch — compiled to native through the SLA toolchain, then registered and executed.
  • Read-only by default: query modules have only read capability by default; writes can only go through the existing single-table transaction API, and modules are not given a surface for writing segment files directly.
  • Fuel metering is a prerequisite, not an optimization: module execution must have a step budget and a timeout. Under the single-writer model, one runaway query can lock up an entire table — without metering, the write path must not ship, and the read-only tier must also be metered to keep a module from hanging the host process.
  • Data files never embed bytecode: data outlives code. Modules live at the application layer and are referenced by hash; persisting stored procedures into the data directory amounts to binding the data to a VM version, and is expressly forbidden.

Risk register

  • A larger TCB with a more sensitive blast radius: the VM interpreter enters db's trust boundary. A Web server worker that crashes can be restarted, but bad bytecode running inside a database can corrupt data — hence the three disciplines of read-only by default, writes through the transaction API, and metering first are all for this.
  • Risk to the performance selling point: interpreted predicate execution being slower than a native scan is the norm, and scan/projection speed is this plugin's main selling point against SQLite. The two-tier design (VM orchestration + native primitives + AOT escape hatch) is the structure that protects the selling point, not optional decoration.
  • Existing interpreter stability issues: the SAB interpreter has registered defects (such as a segfault on & scalar arguments), which are cleanup items on the compiler track; this plan shares that prerequisite bill with the sangx plan.

Recommended steps

  • Step one (read-only tier): predicate/aggregation VM modules over snapshots + native column primitives + fuel metering. Lowest risk, greatest flexibility benefit — new query shapes no longer requiring a plugin release is delivered at this step.
  • Step two (after evaluation): write-procedure modules (through the transaction API) and the AOT registration tier; whether to do it depends on measured data from step one (the module hotness distribution and the share of interpretation overhead).
  • The timing for proposing/planning the project is not yet set; it will be scheduled together with sangx's VM prerequisite work.
